analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent board to police corporate auditors and imposes new penalties and disclosure rules on public companies and their executives.
analysis.headline: After the Enron collapse, Congress passed the bill 334-90 in the House and 99-0 in the Senate, and President Bush signed it into law on July 30, 2002.
analysis.plain_summary: Passed after Enron and other corporate accounting scandals wiped out the savings of employees and investors, this law puts corporate auditors under a new oversight board instead of an industry-run body. It forces CEOs and CFOs to personally certify their companies' financial statements, with prison terms of up to 20 years for willfully certifying false reports. It also bars auditors from selling consulting services to the same companies they audit, bans personal loans from companies to their executives, requires executives to give back bonuses earned on inflated earnings, and protects company whistleblowers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose savings sit in 401(k)s, pensions, and mutual funds invested in public companies. They gain more trustworthy financial statements, auditors with fewer conflicts of interest, longer deadlines to sue over securities fraud, and new protection for employees who report corporate fraud.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board to register, inspect, and discipline the accounting firms that audit public companies, ending a system where the profession policed itself [S5][S6][S7].

Requires the CEO and CFO to personally certify that financial reports are accurate and complete, with criminal penalties of up to 10 years for a knowing false certification and up to 20 years for a willful one [S6][S7].

Bars auditors from performing specified non-audit services for the companies they audit and requires companies' audit committees to preapprove any other services, reducing the financial conflicts that had warped audits at Enron and Andersen [S5][S6].

Requires executives and directors to forfeit bonuses and incentive compensation earned when an accounting restatement caused by a securities-law violation forces their company to restate earnings [S6].
Prohibits corporations from making personal loans to their executives and directors, with limited exceptions for ordinary consumer-credit arrangements [S6].
Extends the deadline for investors to sue over securities fraud to two years after discovery or five years after the violation, whichever comes first [S6].

Prohibits company insiders from trading their stock while employee pension plans are locked in a 'blackout' period, and requires plan administrators to give participants advance notice of blackouts [S6].
Protects employees of publicly traded companies from retaliation for reporting fraud to regulators or Congress, with remedies including reinstatement and back pay [S6][S7].
Boosts SEC funding and staffing for fraud prevention and market oversight, and requires faster disclosure of insider trades by executives and major shareholders [S5][S6].

analysis.who_pays: Public companies bear the cost of new compliance work — executive certifications, internal-control audits, and faster disclosure — and those costs reach shareholders and, in some cases, consumers through higher prices. Accounting firms lose lucrative consulting revenue and pay fees to fund the new oversight board. Executives face personal criminal and financial liability.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public companies, corporate executives, and audit firms

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are substantial, especially for smaller public companies; the Section 404 requirement that auditors attest to management's internal-control assessments became one of the most criticized compliance burdens in securities regulation [S6][S7].

The new oversight board's discipline is limited to intentional or knowing conduct, reckless conduct, or repeated negligent conduct — a single negligent audit cannot be sanctioned on that basis alone [S6].
The board was created as a private nonprofit corporation rather than a government agency, so it is funded by fees on public companies and its members are not federal employees [S7].

The ban on executive loans carves out home-improvement loans, charge cards, and other ordinary consumer-credit arrangements, and the Senate's nonbinding provision asking CEOs to sign corporate tax returns was never made binding [S6].
The bill directed a study of mandatory rotation of audit firms rather than requiring it, leaving the consolidated Big Four firms in place as auditors of nearly all large public companies [S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded real compliance costs and some audit-market disruption for criminal accountability and independent oversight of the industry that certifies the numbers behind every American's retirement savings. The core protections — officer certifications, auditor independence rules, and the new oversight board — directly target the failures that let companies like Enron misstate their finances. The main honest criticism is the cost and rigidity of the internal-control attestation rules, which fell hardest on smaller companies; the law's deeper weaknesses are its carve-outs and its decision to study, rather than adopt, mandatory auditor rotation.

outcome.mechanism: It moved fast: the House passed its version 334-90 in April, the Senate threw out the House text and passed its own much tougher bill 99-0 in July, a conference committee merged the two, and both chambers approved the final version — 423-3 in the House and 99-0 in the Senate — before President Bush signed it on July 30, 2002.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee reported the bill by a 49-12 vote after hearings, and the House passed it on April 24, 2002 by 334-90, with 214 of 221 voting Republicans and 119 of 211 voting Democrats in favor [S3][S9][S11].

Democrats tried to strengthen the House bill: Rep. LaFalce moved to recommit it with instructions — a procedural attempt to send it back for changes — but Republicans voted it down 222-205, with 204 of 211 voting Democrats supporting the motion and 218 of 221 voting Republicans against [S9][S10].

The Senate took up the House bill on July 15, 2002 by unanimous consent, struck the entire House text, and substituted the language of the stronger Sarbanes bill, then passed it by voice vote [S5][S9].

Rep. Conyers moved to instruct House conferees to accept the Senate's tougher provisions, but the motion failed 218-207, with 203 of 211 voting Democrats in favor and 216 of 221 voting Republicans against [S9][S12].
The conference report was approved 423-3 in the House on July 25, 2002, with all 206 voting Democrats and 215 of 218 voting Republicans in favor, and 99-0 in the Senate [S6][S13][S14].
President Bush signed the conference version into law as Public Law 107-204 on July 30, 2002 [S7][S9].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary investors and retirement savers came out ahead: they got independent oversight of auditors and personal accountability for corporate executives, while executives and audit firms lost the looser rules they had operated under.

for.name: Michael G. Oxley
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, guided it through his committee (reported 49-12), and managed it on the House floor and in conference [S8][S9].

for.name: Paul Sarbanes
for.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Authored the stronger Senate companion bill whose language the Senate substituted for the House bill, and served as lead Senate conferee [S5][S9].

for.name: John Conyers
for.what_they_did: Moved to instruct House conferees to accept the Senate's tougher provisions on document destruction, bankruptcy protection, and the fraud statute of limitations; the motion failed 218-207 [S9][S12].

for.name: John LaFalce
for.role: Ranking Member, House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the House bill with instructions to add stronger investor protections before final passage; the motion failed 222-205 [S9][S10].

for.name: George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on July 30, 2002 [S9].

against.name: 218 of 223 House Republicans
against.role: House Republican bloc on the motion to recommit
against.what_they_did: Voted down the motion to recommit the bill to add stronger investor protections, allowing the weaker House version to move forward [S10].

against.name: 216 of 223 House Republicans
against.role: House Republican bloc on the motion to instruct conferees
against.what_they_did: Voted down the Conyers motion directing House conferees to accept the Senate's stricter criminal and investor-protection provisions [S12].

against.name: American Institute of Certified Public Accountants
against.role: Trade association for the accounting profession
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against creating an independent public board to oversee auditors, favoring continued industry self-regulation.

sides.party_line_note: The final votes were nearly unanimous — 423-3 in the House and 99-0 in the Senate — but every attempt to strengthen the bill along the way split sharply by party: Democrats voted 204-3 and 203-1 to add or preserve the tougher protections, while Republicans voted 218-0 and 216-3 to defeat them [S10][S11][S12].

industries.note: The law strips auditors of the consulting work that had compromised their independence, subjects them to registration, inspections, and discipline by the new oversight board, and makes their fraud debts nondischargeable in bankruptcy. It leaves the highly consolidated Big Four firms in place as auditors of nearly all large public companies — the bill ordered a study of mandatory rotation instead of requiring it.

industries.industry: Corporate executives and directors of public companies
industries.note: Executives must personally certify financial reports under threat of prison, forfeit bonuses after fraud-driven restatements, and can be barred from serving as officers or directors; their companies can no longer lend them money. Their interest in lax personal accountability ran directly against the investors the bill protects.

The SEC must adopt rules separating analysts from investment-banking pressure, barring retaliation for unfavorable research and requiring conflict disclosures. This ends the practice of banks inflating research reports to win fees at the expense of small investors.

Companies absorb significant compliance costs — certifications, internal-control audits, faster disclosure — which reach shareholders. Shareholders also get more reliable financial statements and longer windows to sue over fraud.
